{{distinguish|Banach–Mazur distance|Banach–Mazur game}}
In [[functional analysis]], a field of [[mathematics]], a key object of study is a [[normed space]], which is a [[vector space]] equipped with a [[norm (mathematics)|norm]], which allows vectors to be measured. When they are [[infinite dimensional]], normed spaces can be very complicated. A standard normed space is the space <math>C([0,1],\mathbb R)</math> of [[continuous function]]s on the [[unit interval]], <math>f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R</math>, which is equipped with the norm <math>\|f\| = \max_{x\in [0,1]}|f(x)|</math>, the [[maximum value]] of the function.

The '''Banach–Mazur theorem''' is a [[theorem]] that provides one way of bounding the complexity of certain [[well-behaved]] normed spaces ([[separable space|separable]]).  It states that every such normed space can be embedded into the normed space <math>C([0,1],\mathbb R)</math>, in such a way that the norm (length) of every vector is preserved (a property known as an [[isometry]]). It is named after [[Stefan Banach]] and [[Stanisław Mazur]].

==Statement==
Every [[real number|real]], [[separable space|separable]] [[Banach space]] {{math|(''X'', {{!!}}&nbsp;⋅&nbsp;{{!!}})}} is [[Isometry|isometrically isomorphic]] to a [[Closed set|closed]] subspace of {{math|C<sup>0</sup>([0, 1], '''R''')}}, the space of all [[continuous function]]s from the unit [[Interval (mathematics)|interval]] into the real line.

==Comments==
On the one hand, the Banach–Mazur theorem seems to tell us that the seemingly vast collection of all separable Banach spaces is not that vast or difficult to work with, since a separable Banach space is "only" a collection of continuous paths. On the other hand, the theorem tells us that {{math|C<sup>0</sup>([0, 1], '''R''')}} is a "really big" space, big enough to contain every possible separable Banach space.

Non-separable Banach spaces cannot embed isometrically in the separable space {{math|C<sup>0</sup>([0, 1], '''R''')}}, but for every Banach space {{mvar|X}}, one can find a [[compact space|compact]] [[Hausdorff space]] {{mvar|K}} and an isometric linear embedding {{mvar|j}} of {{mvar|X}} into the space {{math|C(''K'')}} of scalar continuous functions on {{mvar|K}}. The simplest choice is to let {{mvar|K}} be the [[Unit sphere|unit ball]] of the [[Dual space#Continuous dual space|continuous dual]] {{math|''X''&thinsp;′}}, equipped with the [[Weak topology|w*-topology]]. This unit ball {{mvar|K}} is then compact by the [[Banach–Alaoglu theorem]]. The embedding {{mvar|j}} is introduced by saying that for every {{math|''x'' ∈ ''X''}}, the continuous function {{math|''j''(''x'')}} on {{mvar|K}} is defined by

:<math> \forall x' \in K: \qquad j(x)(x') = x'(x).</math>

The mapping {{mvar|j}} is linear, and it is isometric by the [[Hahn–Banach theorem]].

Another generalization was given by Kleiber and Pervin (1969): a [[metric space]] of [[dense set|density]] equal to an infinite cardinal {{mvar|α}} is isometric to a subspace of {{math|C<sup>0</sup>([0,1]<sup>α</sup>, '''R''')}}, the space of real continuous functions on the [[Cartesian product#Infinite products|product]] of {{mvar|α}} copies of the unit interval.

==Stronger versions of the theorem==
Let us write {{math|C<sup>''k''</sup>[0, 1]}} for {{math|C<sup>''k''</sup>([0, 1], '''R''')}}. In 1995, Luis Rodríguez-Piazza proved that the isometry {{math|''i'' : ''X'' → C<sup>0</sup>[0, 1]}} can be chosen so that every non-zero function in the [[image (mathematics)|image]] {{math|''i''(''X'')}} is [[nowhere differentiable]]. Put another way, if {{math|''D'' ⊂ C<sup>0</sup>[0, 1]}} consists of functions that are differentiable at at least one point of {{math|[0, 1]}}, then {{mvar|i}} can be chosen so that {{math|''i''(''X'') ∩ ''D'' {{=}} {0}.}} This conclusion applies to the space {{math|C<sup>0</sup>[0, 1]}} itself, hence there exists a [[linear map]] {{math|''i'' : C<sup>0</sup>[0, 1] → C<sup>0</sup>[0, 1]}} that is an isometry onto its image, such that image under {{mvar|i}} of {{math|C<sup>0</sup>[0, 1]}} (the subspace consisting of functions that are everywhere differentiable with continuous derivative) intersects {{mvar|D}} only at {{math|0}}: thus the space of smooth functions (with respect to the uniform distance) is isometrically isomorphic to a space of nowhere-differentiable functions. Note that the (metrically incomplete) space of smooth functions is dense in {{math|C<sup>0</sup>[0, 1]}}.
